hints: Look closely at the two ends of a tRNA molecule in the cloverleaf diagram, one end holds the amino acid and the opposite loop faces the mRNA on the ribosome.
Remember how mRNA codons and tRNA anticodons pair up, and remember RNA uses uracil (U) while DNA uses thymine (T), so can they ever be exactly the same?
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 - two different jobs**

Think of tRNA as an adaptor with two ends. The 3' end has a CCA site where a specific amino acid attaches.

The other end has the anticodon loop which pairs with the mRNA codon when the tRNA sits on the ribosome. So statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2 - backbone and folding**

Like all RNA, tRNA has a ribose-phosphate backbone joined by strong phosphodiester bonds.

The single chain folds back on itself to form the cloverleaf shape, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. So statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3 - same versus complementary**

This is the tricky one. The mRNA codon is complementary to the DNA template that was transcribed.

The tRNA anticodon is then complementary to the mRNA codon, not identical to the DNA triplet. Also RNA has U, DNA has T, so they cannot be the same. So statement 3 is incorrect.

Correct statements are 1 and 2 only, which is option B.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes statement 3, which is false as the anticodon is complementary to the mRNA codon, not the same as the DNA triplet.
options.B: Correct because statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, so 1 and 2 only is the right combination.
options.C: Incorrect because although statement 1 is true, it wrongly leaves out statement 2 which correctly describes the backbone and internal base pairing.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes the false statement 3 and wrongly leaves out the true statement 1.
